newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil stocks seen choppy now, rising long-term.
newsitem.headline: Brazil stocks seen choppy now, rising long-term.

text.p: Brazilian shares will be subject to volatility short-term, but equity analysts are confident that in a matter of weeks the Sao Paulo bolsa will resume a steady uptrend and gain moderately by year's end.
Analysts believe it will take a few days before the bolsa stabilizes and gains further terrain after dropping last week amid rollercoaster-like trade.
"It may remain volatile, treading water for the next ten days," said Alvaro Maia, head of equities sales at Caspian Securities in Brazil.
But the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange is unlikely to repeat the spectacular performance that marked trading in the first half of 1997, analysts said.
"We see an upside of between 18 percent to 20 percent until the end of the year," said Maia. "The rise will be much more moderate from now on."

Local shares, which had made gains of over 80 percent until early July, plunged 15 percent in just five sessions in a profit-taking frenzy led by local stock funds, which until then had been the driving force behind the market's surge.
Last week's slump reduced the bolsa's cumulative rise to 58.8 percent so far this year.

The profit-taking, which most analysts said should be expected after the bolsa's stunning gains since the beginning of the year, was triggered by fears that Brazil could also become the target of currency speculators who in recent weeks forced some Asian countries to devalue.
Maia said the market should stabilize at new levels as soon as domestic equity funds figure out how many investors stay in stocks and how many walk away from equities.

Most investors who exited the funds -- which just last Wednesday saw net outflows of 501.3 million reais -- were relatively small investors used to the safety of fixed-income funds who moved into equities seeking higher returns.
With domestic interest rates declining, no other local investment has provided yields as high as the stock market.
Asset managers believe that fund redemptions will no longer be that significant, easing the selling pressure on the bolsa.
"Those who were not familiar with stock volatility may have already exited the funds," said Orestes Prado, director at the National Association of Investment Bankers (ANBID).
Considering the share price depreciation, combined stock fund assets fell to 18.1 billion reais from about 19 billion reais before last week's slump, according to latest bank statistics.
Prado estimates a further 100 million reais left the funds on Friday, when traders reported heavy selling by fund managers to cover anticipated withdrawals by retail investors.
Analysts think local stock funds will play a lesser role in the market during the second half as many small investors have become gun-shy and will eschew the funds.

In the last six months of the year, the bolsa is more likely to rise on the country's fundamentals: upcoming privatizations, particularly in telecommunications and energy, progress on constitutional reforms, and corporate earnings, they said.
